len.title: How str::len works
len.description: The length in bytes, which is not always the number of characters.

slides.caption: Rust strings are UTF-8. Plain letters take 1 byte; letters like é take 2.
l, l and o are 1 byte each.
5 characters, but len() is 6. Use s.chars().count() to count characters.

chars.title: How str::chars works
chars.description: An iterator over the characters (Unicode scalar values) of a string.

slides.caption: chars() decodes the UTF-8 bytes and yields one char at a time.
'é' is one char, even though it takes 2 bytes.
chars() gives 5 items for "héllo", while len() says 6 bytes. Some symbols (like emoji with skin tones) are several chars.

char_indices.title: How str::char_indices works
char_indices.description: Each character together with its byte position.

slides.caption: char_indices yields (byte index, char) pairs. The index is where the char starts in the bytes.
'é' starts at byte 1 and takes bytes 1 and 2.
So the next 'l' starts at byte 3, not 2.
These byte indexes are the ones you may use for slicing: &s[3..] is "llo".

split.title: How str::split works
split.description: Cuts a string at every separator; empty pieces are kept.

slides.caption: split(',') cuts at every comma and yields the pieces between them.
Between two commas in a row there is nothing: an empty piece "".
Empty pieces are kept on purpose. Add .filter(|s| !s.is_empty()) to drop them, or use split_whitespace for spaces.

split_whitespace.title: How str::split_whitespace works
split_whitespace.description: Splits at any run of spaces, tabs or newlines; never yields empty pieces.

slides.caption: split_whitespace treats any run of whitespace as one separator and ignores it at both ends.
Three spaces in a row count as one separator.
"you", and the trailing space is ignored.
Perfect for reading words from input. Compare split(' '), which would give empty pieces here.

lines.title: How str::lines works
lines.description: Splits a string into lines; handles both \n and \r\n.

note.text: the line endings are not included

slides.caption: lines() cuts at each line ending (shown as ↵) and drops it.
The second line is "two". A final line ending does not create an empty line.
lines() also removes the \r of Windows line endings, so "a\r\nb" gives "a", "b".

trim.title: How str::trim works
trim.description: Removes whitespace from both ends; returns a slice of the same string.

slides.caption: trim finds the first and last non-whitespace characters and returns what is between them.
What is left is "hi": a view into the original string.
trim returns &str borrowed from the original. trim_start and trim_end cut only one side.

starts_with.title: How str::starts_with works
starts_with.description: Checks whether the string begins with a given text.

slides.caption: starts_with compares the first characters with the pattern.
The first 4 characters are "rust", exactly the pattern.
So the answer is true. The rest is not looked at.
The pattern can also be a char or a closure: s.starts_with(char::is_uppercase). ends_with checks the end.

contains.title: How str::contains works
contains.description: Checks whether a text appears anywhere in the string.

note.text: anywhere, not just at the start

slides.caption: contains searches the whole string for the pattern.
"o w" is found starting at position 4.
contains only says whether it exists: true.
Use find to also learn where it is. The search is case-sensitive: "Hello".contains("hello") is false.

find.title: How str::find works
find.description: Returns the byte index where a pattern first appears.

note.text: the first match from the left

slides.caption: find looks for "an" from the left and returns where the first match starts.
At index 1, "an" matches: the answer is Some(1).
rfind searches from the right ("banana".rfind("an") is Some(3)). None means not found.

split_once.title: How str::split_once works
split_once.description: Splits at the first separator into exactly two parts.

slides.caption: split_once cuts at the first separator only and returns the part before and the part after.
The first = is at index 3. Before it: "key".
Everything after it is the second part, including the second =.
Ideal for "key=value" lines. Without a separator it returns None. rsplit_once cuts at the last one.

splitn.title: How str::splitn works
splitn.description: Splits at most into n pieces; the last piece keeps the rest.

slides.caption: splitn(2, ...) makes at most one cut, so there are at most 2 pieces.
That was the one allowed cut: the rest stays together, dashes included.
splitn(1, x) never cuts at all.

parse.title: How str::parse works
parse.description: Converts text into another type; returns a Result because it can fail.

slides.caption: parse reads the text and tries to build the type you ask for, here i32.
"4x" is not: Err, with a ParseIntError explaining why.
Handle the Result: "42".parse::<i32>()? in a function, or .unwrap_or(0) for a default. Spaces are not allowed: trim first.

strip_prefix.title: How str::strip_prefix works
strip_prefix.description: Removes a prefix if it is there; returns None if it is not.

slides.caption: strip_prefix checks the start and returns the rest only when the prefix matches.
The string starts with 'v': it is removed.
If the prefix is missing you get None, so you know. trim_start_matches would silently do nothing (or remove several).

get.title: How str::get works
get.description: Slices safely by byte range: None instead of a panic.

slides.caption: Byte 2 is in the middle of é (bytes 1 and 2). Slicing there would cut a character in half.
Bytes 0..2 would be h plus half of é.
&s[0..2] would panic. get(0..2) returns None instead.
get(0..3) is Some("hé"). When ranges come from char_indices, they always fall on boundaries.

bytes.title: How str::bytes works
bytes.description: An iterator over the raw UTF-8 bytes of a string.

slides.caption: bytes() yields the u8 values that store the string.
Use bytes() for ASCII data or byte-level work; chars() for text.

trim_start.title: How str::trim_start works
trim_start.description: Removes whitespace at the start only.

slides.caption: trim_start cuts whitespace from the beginning.
The two leading spaces are cut off.
trim_end does the other side; trim does both.

trim_end.title: How str::trim_end works
trim_end.description: Removes whitespace at the end only, such as a trailing newline.

slides.caption: Lines read from input often end with a newline (↵). trim_end removes it.
The newline at the end is whitespace: removed.
Always trim input before parsing: "42\n".parse::<i32>() fails, "42" works.

ends_with.title: How str::ends_with works
ends_with.description: Checks whether the string ends with a given text.

slides.caption: ends_with compares the last characters with the pattern.
Case matters: "PHOTO.PNG".ends_with(".png") is false. For paths, std::path::Path::extension is more robust.

rfind.title: How str::rfind works
rfind.description: The byte index of the last match of a pattern.

slides.caption: rfind finds the last occurrence, but the index still counts from the left.
Searching from the right, the first / found is at index 3.
The other / at index 1 is never reached.
To take everything after it: &s[i + 1..] is "c". rsplit_once('/') does both in one step.

strip_suffix.title: How str::strip_suffix works
strip_suffix.description: Removes a suffix if it is there; None if it is not.

slides.caption: strip_suffix checks the end and returns the part before it.
Returns None when the suffix is missing, so you can tell the two cases apart.

rsplit_once.title: How str::rsplit_once works
rsplit_once.description: Splits at the last separator into two parts.

slides.caption: rsplit_once cuts at the last separator.

matches.title: How str::matches works
matches.description: An iterator over every match of a pattern.

slides.caption: matches yields every piece of the string that matches the pattern.
With a string pattern, s.matches("ab").count() counts how often "ab" appears (without overlaps).

eq_ignore_ascii_case.title: How str::eq_ignore_ascii_case works
eq_ignore_ascii_case.description: Compares two strings, treating upper and lower case ASCII letters as equal.

slides.caption: Each pair of characters is compared after lowering A–Z.
Y/y, e/E, s/S: equal when case is ignored.

eq.text: y = y, e = e, s = s

slides.caption: Cheaper than a.to_lowercase() == b.to_lowercase(), which allocates two Strings.

split_terminator.title: How str::split_terminator works
split_terminator.description: Like split, but a separator at the very end makes no empty piece.

slides.caption: With split(';') you would get "a", "b" and an empty "".
"b", and the final ; ends the list.
Good for formats where every item ends with a separator.

rsplit.title: How str::rsplit works
rsplit.description: Splits like split, but yields the pieces from right to left.

slides.caption: rsplit starts at the end of the string.
rsplit('.').next() is a quick way to get the last part.

trim_matches.title: How str::trim_matches works
trim_matches.description: Removes a pattern repeatedly from both ends.

slides.caption: trim_matches keeps cutting the pattern off both ends while it matches.
trim_start_matches and trim_end_matches do one side. The pattern can be a closure: trim_matches(char::is_numeric).

match_indices.title: How str::match_indices works
match_indices.description: Every match together with its byte position.

slides.caption: Useful for highlighting all occurrences of a word.

split_at.title: How str::split_at works
split_at.description: Cuts a string at a byte position into two slices.

slides.caption: split_at(2) returns the part before byte 2 and the part from byte 2 on.
Panics if the position is inside a multi-byte character; split_at_checked returns None instead.

is_char_boundary.title: How str::is_char_boundary works
is_char_boundary.description: Checks whether a byte index starts a character.

slides.caption: é uses bytes 0 and 1; ! starts at byte 2.
Byte 1 is in the middle of é: false.
Check this before slicing with an index you computed yourself.

as_bytes.title: How str::as_bytes works
as_bytes.description: Views the string as its UTF-8 bytes, without copying.

slides.caption: as_bytes gives a byte slice of the same memory.
b"Hi" is a byte-string literal with the same bytes.

is_empty.title: How str::is_empty works
is_empty.description: true when the string has no bytes.

slides.caption: is_empty checks the length, not whether the text looks blank.

rsplitn.title: How str::rsplitn works
rsplitn.description: Splits from the right into at most n pieces.

note.text: cut only at the last dot

slides.caption: rsplitn(2, ...) makes one cut, starting from the right.
rsplit_once('.') gives the same two parts as a tuple.
Only the two lowercase words are accepted.
For yes/no input, match on s.to_lowercase().as_str() yourself.

as_str.title: How Chars::as_str works
as_str.description: The part of the string the iterator has not reached yet.

slides.caption: Chars walks through the string; as_str shows the remaining text without copying.
Handy in parsers: read a few chars, then look at the rest as a &str.

offset.title: How CharIndices::offset works
offset.description: The byte position of the next character.

slides.caption: After a (1 byte) and é (2 bytes), the next char starts at byte 3.
Use it to slice the string right after what you have read.

trim_start_matches.title: How str::trim_start_matches works
trim_start_matches.description: Removes a pattern from the start, as often as it repeats.

slides.caption: Every leading match goes; the zero inside 420 stays.
strip_prefix removes the pattern at most once.

trim_end_matches.title: How str::trim_end_matches works
trim_end_matches.description: Removes a pattern from the end, as often as it repeats.

slides.caption: The pattern can be a str, a char, a list of chars or a closure.

rmatches.title: How str::rmatches works
rmatches.description: Every match of a pattern, from the end backwards.

slides.caption: Same matches as matches(), in reverse order.

rmatch_indices.title: How str::rmatch_indices works
rmatch_indices.description: Every match with its byte position, from the end backwards.

slides.caption: Useful for finding the last occurrences first.
rfind gives only the last position.

split_ascii_whitespace.title: How str::split_ascii_whitespace works
split_ascii_whitespace.description: Splits at runs of ASCII spaces, tabs and newlines.

slides.caption: Runs of whitespace count as one separator; no empty pieces.

escape_debug.title: How str::escape_debug works
escape_debug.description: The text with special characters escaped, as {:?} shows it.

slides.caption: Each special character becomes a backslash sequence.
Printable Unicode such as é is kept; escape_default escapes it too.
Handy when the output must be plain ASCII, like some config files.

escape_unicode.title: How str::escape_unicode works
escape_unicode.description: Writes every character as a \u{…} escape.

slides.caption: Each char becomes its Unicode number in hex.
Useful to see exactly which characters a string contains.

make_ascii_uppercase.title: How str::make_ascii_uppercase works
make_ascii_uppercase.description: Upper-cases ASCII letters in place, without a new String.

slides.caption: The bytes are changed where they are; the length never changes.
i, d and x become I, D and X.
Works on a String or a &mut str.
Good for normalising file extensions before comparing.

is_ascii.title: How str::is_ascii works
is_ascii.description: true if every character is plain ASCII.

slides.caption: If true, every char is exactly one byte, so byte indexes and char indexes agree.
Check it before using fast byte-based tricks on text.

get_mut.title: How str::get_mut works
get_mut.description: A mutable sub-slice, or None if the range is invalid.

slides.caption: The range must lie on character boundaries, otherwise you get None (no panic).
Only in-place, same-length changes are possible on a &mut str.

trim_ascii.title: How str::trim_ascii works
trim_ascii.description: Removes ASCII whitespace from both ends.

slides.caption: Like trim, but only spaces, tabs and newlines from ASCII count.
Tab and space at the start go.
Space and newline at the end go.
trim also removes Unicode spaces such as the no-break space.

split_inclusive.title: How str::split_inclusive works
split_inclusive.description: Splits after each separator, keeping it at the end of its piece.

slides.caption: Each piece ends with the separator that closed it.

encode_utf16.title: How str::encode_utf16 works
encode_utf16.description: The text as UTF-16 code units, as Windows and JavaScript use.

slides.caption: Most characters take one u16; characters beyond U+FFFF take two (a surrogate pair).
String::from_utf16 goes back the other way.

rsplit_terminator.title: How str::rsplit_terminator works
rsplit_terminator.description: Like rsplit, but a separator at the very end makes no empty piece.

slides.caption: The final ; terminates the last item instead of starting an empty one.

split_at_checked.title: How str::split_at_checked works
split_at_checked.description: split_at that returns None instead of panicking.

slides.caption: Byte 2 is in the middle of é, so splitting there is impossible.
Byte 2 is not a char boundary: None.
Use it when the position comes from user input or a computation.

from_utf8.title: How str::from_utf8 works
from_utf8.description: Views bytes as a &str, if they are valid UTF-8.

slides.caption: The bytes are checked, not copied.
String::from_utf8 does the same for an owned Vec<u8>.

next.title: How Chars::next works
next.description: Decodes the next character of the string.

slides.caption: Chars reads UTF-8: é takes two bytes but comes out as one char.
s.chars().next() is the usual way to get the first character.

count.title: How Chars::count works
count.description: The number of characters, which can differ from the number of bytes.

slides.caption: é is one character but two bytes.
Counting chars walks the whole string; len() is instant.

last.title: How Chars::last works
last.description: The last character of the string.

slides.caption: Chars::last reads backwards from the end instead of walking the whole string.

next_back.title: How Chars::next_back works
next_back.description: Decodes the next character from the end.

slides.caption: Chars can walk from both ends; chars().rev() uses this.

char_indices-next.title: How CharIndices::next works
char_indices-next.description: The next character together with its byte position.

slides.caption: Byte positions jump by the size of each character.
The indexes are safe to slice with: &s[i..].
Each of these characters takes 3 bytes, but there are only 2 characters.

char_indices-last.title: How CharIndices::last works
char_indices-last.description: The last character and its byte position.

char_indices-next_back.title: How CharIndices::next_back works
char_indices-next_back.description: The next character from the end, with its byte position.

slides.caption: char_indices().rev() walks the string backwards with positions.
Find the last space: s.char_indices().rev().find(|(_, c)| *c == ' ').

bytes_iter-next.title: How Bytes::next works
bytes_iter-next.description: The next byte of the string's UTF-8 encoding.

slides.caption: Use chars() for characters, bytes() for raw data.

bytes_iter-count.title: How Bytes::count works
bytes_iter-count.description: The number of bytes left; instant.

slides.caption: A byte iterator knows its length.
s.len() gives the same number directly.

nth.title: How Bytes::nth works
nth.description: The byte at a position (skipping the ones before).

slides.caption: s.as_bytes().get(1) does the same without consuming anything.

any.title: How Bytes::any works
any.description: true if some byte passes the test.

slides.caption: Stops at the first matching byte.
The bytes are checked in order.

position.title: How Bytes::position works
position.description: The index of the first byte that passes the test.

slides.caption: Positions are byte offsets, safe to slice with when the byte is ASCII.
k, e, y do not match.

rposition.title: How Bytes::rposition works
rposition.description: The index of the last byte that passes the test.

all.title: How Bytes::all works
all.description: true if every byte passes the test.

slides.caption: Stops at the first byte that fails.

bytes_iter-rfind.title: How Bytes::rfind works
bytes_iter-rfind.description: The last byte that passes the test.

slides.caption: Searches backwards: 2 and 1 fail, b passes.
Returns the byte; rposition returns its index.

split_iter-next.title: How next works on s.split(..)
split_iter-next.description: Gives the next piece of a split string.

slides.caption: The same next() serves split, rsplit, split_terminator, matches and more: they are all generated by one macro.
Grab just the first field: s.split(',').next().

split_iter-next_back.title: How next_back works on s.split(..)
split_iter-next_back.description: Gives the next piece from the end.

slides.caption: Splitting can be walked from either end.

lines_iter-next.title: How Lines::next works
lines_iter-next.description: Gives the next line, without its line ending.

slides.caption: Both Windows and Unix line endings are handled.

lines_iter-last.title: How Lines::last works
lines_iter-last.description: The last line of the text.

note.text: a trailing \n adds no empty line

slides.caption: Useful for the last line of a log.

split_whitespace_iter-next.title: How SplitWhitespace::next works
split_whitespace_iter-next.description: Gives the next word, skipping any amount of whitespace.

slides.caption: Leading, trailing and repeated spaces are all skipped.
The first word of a command: s.split_whitespace().next().
The words are the, quick, fox.
Reads backwards, so it is quick even for long text.

floor_char_boundary.title: How str::floor_char_boundary works
floor_char_boundary.description: The nearest character boundary at or before a byte index.

slides.caption: Byte 2 is inside é, so it moves back to where é starts.
Byte 2 is in the middle of é.

ceil_char_boundary.title: How str::ceil_char_boundary works
ceil_char_boundary.description: The nearest character boundary at or after a byte index.

slides.caption: Byte 2 is inside é, so it moves forward to where l starts.
Pair with floor_char_boundary for safe slicing.

split_at_mut.title: How str::split_at_mut works
split_at_mut.description: Two mutable halves of a string, split at a byte index.

slides.caption: Each half can be changed separately (same-length changes only).
Only the first half is upper-cased.
Panics if the index is not on a char boundary.

split_at_mut_checked.title: How str::split_at_mut_checked works
split_at_mut_checked.description: split_at_mut that returns None instead of panicking.

trim_ascii_start.title: How str::trim_ascii_start works
trim_ascii_start.description: Removes ASCII whitespace from the start only.

trim_ascii_end.title: How str::trim_ascii_end works
trim_ascii_end.description: Removes ASCII whitespace from the end only.

from_utf8_mut.title: How str::from_utf8_mut works
from_utf8_mut.description: Views mutable bytes as a &mut str, if they are valid UTF-8.

slides.caption: The bytes are checked once, then edited as a string.
Err if the bytes are not valid UTF-8.

utf8_chunks.title: How utf8_chunks works
utf8_chunks.description: Splits bytes into valid text pieces and the invalid bytes between them.

title.text: for c in bytes.utf8_chunks() { c.valid(); c.invalid(); }

slides.caption: Each chunk has a valid part and the invalid bytes right after it.

valid.title: How Utf8Chunk::valid works
valid.description: The valid UTF-8 text at the start of a chunk.

slides.caption: Everything up to the first invalid byte.
invalid() gives the broken bytes after it.

invalid.title: How Utf8Chunk::invalid works
invalid.description: The invalid bytes that end a chunk.

slides.caption: 0xC0 can never appear in valid UTF-8.
Replace it with � or report its position.

valid_up_to.title: How Utf8Error::valid_up_to works
valid_up_to.description: How many bytes at the start are valid UTF-8.

error_len.title: How Utf8Error::error_len works
error_len.description: How many bytes are invalid; None if the input just ended too early.

slides.caption: 0xFF is always invalid; 0xC3 is a valid start that needs another byte.
0xC3 at the end: maybe more bytes are coming, None.
None matters when reading a stream in pieces.

char_indices-as_str.title: How CharIndices::as_str works
char_indices-as_str.description: The text not yet visited by char_indices().

slides.caption: No copy: it borrows from the original.

as_ptr.title: How str::as_ptr works
as_ptr.description: A raw pointer to the first byte of the string.

slides.caption: Not NUL-terminated: use CString for C APIs.
Pair with len() when passing to other code.

as_bytes_mut.title: How str::as_bytes_mut works
as_bytes_mut.description: Mutable access to the string's bytes (unsafe).

slides.caption: The text must stay valid UTF-8.
make_ascii_uppercase is the safe way here.

as_mut_ptr.title: How str::as_mut_ptr works
as_mut_ptr.description: A raw mutable pointer to the string's bytes.

slides.caption: Writes must keep the text valid UTF-8.

get_unchecked.title: How str::get_unchecked works
get_unchecked.description: A substring by byte range without checks (unsafe).

slides.caption: The range must be in bounds and on char boundaries.

get_unchecked_mut.title: How str::get_unchecked_mut works
get_unchecked_mut.description: A mutable substring by byte range without checks (unsafe).

slides.caption: Range must be valid and on boundaries.

from_utf8_assoc.title: How str::from_utf8 (associated function) works
from_utf8_assoc.description: Views bytes as &str if valid UTF-8, written as str::from_utf8.

slides.caption: Same as std::str::from_utf8, as an associated function.

from_utf8_mut_assoc.title: How str::from_utf8_mut (associated function) works
from_utf8_mut_assoc.description: Views mutable bytes as &mut str if valid UTF-8.

slides.caption: The checked version returns a Result.

from_utf8_unchecked_mut_assoc.title: How str::from_utf8_unchecked_mut (associated function) works
from_utf8_unchecked_mut_assoc.description: Views mutable bytes as &mut str without checking (unsafe).

slides.caption: Undefined behaviour if not valid UTF-8.

from_utf8_unchecked_mut.title: How str::from_utf8_unchecked_mut works
from_utf8_unchecked_mut.description: Views mutable bytes as &mut str without validating (unsafe).

strip_circumfix.title: How str::strip_circumfix works
strip_circumfix.description: Removes a prefix and a suffix together, if both are present.

slides.caption: None if either end does not match.

substr_range.title: How str::substr_range works
substr_range.description: The byte range of a substring within the string, if it belongs to it.

slides.caption: Useful for error messages pointing into input.
